correctness.rationale: Kummer counts the carries in n+2n. A first carry requires two adjacent 1 bits of n and forces the next carry because the shifted summand then has bit 1 and there is an incoming carry. A string of s ones, s>=2, gives exactly s carries, continuing through the high shifted bit; dyadic scaling leaves the count unchanged. Splitting even and odd factors gives B_{2N}/B_N=O(6N)/(O(2N)O(4N)), where O is the odd factorial part. For N=2^t a and fixed modulus, the complete odd-residue blocks have products 1 at large t (units pair by inversion; the self-inverse units multiply to 1 for k>=3; for k=2 take an even number of blocks). Therefore B_{2^t a} stabilizes at each modulus, defining U_a with the same valuation as B_a. In the exact factorial ratio B_{A+H}/(B_A B_H), the factors and inverse factors are 1+cH/j with c in {1,2,3}; for A=2^t a, H=2^(t+r)b and j<=3A, v2(j)<=t+floor(log2(3a)). The prescribed gap makes every ratio factor a unit congruent to 1 mod 2^k, so this use of ratios is valid even when B_A or B_H itself is not a unit. Passing to the limits and repeating realizes a finite product of U values at positive indices. U_1=7 and U_9=5 modulo 8; exact seed residues follow from B_8 and B_72 and stabilization modulo 8. The valuation of U_9^(2^j)-1 is j+2 by successive factorization, giving the entire subgroup 1 mod 4, and U_1 supplies its other unit coset. This works at k=1,2 with the respective trivial or order-two groups. Multiplying a seed of valuation s>=2 by units gives every class of that valuation; a sufficiently high valuation gives zero. Stabilizing at positive dyadic multiples supplies infinitely many indices for each class. This proves the count, two-adic closure and Haar measure, with no frequency assertion. Independent replay: python3 /workspace/independent_checks.py 3 used an exact consecutive-index factorial ratio checked against direct binomial evaluations and enumerated n=0..32767; it attained precisely the allowed sets for k=1..8 and checked seed residues 7 and 5. The finite image is not the all-k proof.
